ingredients.item: whole squid , bodies 15–20 cm, cleaned, skins peeled, tentacles separated
coarse salt and a light grind of pepper
soy sauce , 1 tbsp rice vinegar , 1 tsp gochugaru , 1 tsp sesame seeds , 1 scallion sliced, 1/2 Korean chili or jalapeño sliced into rings
Steamed rice , soju or beer's ceremony, mu sangchae to cut the heat

instructions.heading: Dry-grill first, glaze second
instructions.action: Dry-grill first, glaze second. The scored bodies go on scored-face-down over the hot fire, tentacles beside them. Ninety seconds undisturbed — the bodies will curl and the scores will gape open, toasting in their grooves; the tentacle tips will char at their edges.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the scored face shows toasted brown in the grooves with light char at the curling edges; the smell is sweet-iodine ocean toast (this is correct — squid's smell on fire should be oceanic, never sulfurous; a sulfurous fish-market smell means the squid was past its day). If the bodies stick, the grate was not hot enough — a hot grate releases squid the way it releases skin.

instructions.heading: Flip, glaze, finish
instructions.action: Flip, glaze, finish. Turn the bodies and tentacles, brush the toasted faces with glaze, 45–60 seconds more, and a second thin brush-stroke over each. The glaze needs only to set glossy — it is not cooking, it is dressing.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the glaze foams lightly and turns brick-glossy. Pull the bodies when they are just firm to the touch — springy with give, not tight as a drum. Tight-as-drum is the rubber door, and it closes at about the four-minute mark for bodies this size.

instructions.heading: Cut at the table
instructions.action: Cut at the table. The scissors are the service: bodies crosswise into wide rings (the scored blossoms open as you cut), tentacles in halves. Straight from the board into the dip, or over rice with the glaze's drippings.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: eating test, a ring straight from the dip: snap-tender bite (the 2-minute squid's signature), char in the score grooves, the glaze's sweet-heat, the dip's vinegar and chili behind it. Any rubbery chew means some piece crossed the doneness line — pull earlier next batch; squid cannot be saved, only timed.

visualDonenessCues: The squid: cleaned, skinned, inner-face crosshatch at 5 mm, bone-dry before the fire.
The grill: hot and close (about 250 °C at the surface), dry sear first, glaze after the flip only.
The pull: scored face toasted, glaze glossy, body springy-with-give before the four-minute mark.
The table: scissors to rings, dip ready before the fire, cold drinks standing by — the dish's whole grammar.
storageNotes: Raw squid keeps 1 day on ice; glaze and dip keep a week (the dip improves). Cooked rings keep 1 day and make a fierce stir-fried rice or noodle addition, reheated hard and fast — remember, this record is the 2-minute pole of squid's doneness law; the 2-hour pole is a different dish entirely (braised ojingeo-jjim, not this record).

Variations: the clean-lane fork skips the glaze for soy-garlic baste and the #SF02 register; baby octopus runs this same glaze on the jjukkumi record (#SF06); the dip doubles as the sauce for cold boiled eggs, a pojangmacha two-fer.
